strengths: Reveals a clean product-manifold structure underlying the Cholesky (diagonal log) metric, providing a principled and extensible framework for designing new SPD metrics by choosing different metrics on R++.

Derives full closed-form Riemannian operators (geodesic, Log/Exp, parallel transport, weighted Fréchet mean) and gyrovector structures for the two proposed metrics (PCM, BWCM), matching or exceeding the operator coverage of existing metrics like BWM/GBWM which lack some closed forms.
Provides a deformation family connecting the new metrics to the existing diagonal-log/LCM metric, offering a tunable interpolation and theoretical unification.

Comprehensive empirical validation across multiple axes: classification accuracy/efficiency on SPDNet, GyroSPD and RResNet backbones over three datasets, explicit numerical stability stress tests (small eigenvalues), asymptotic and empirical scalability analysis, and tensor interpolation visualizations.
Theoretical rigor: explicit proofs of theorems (isometry-based derivations, gyrogroup/gyrovector space axioms) are given in the appendix, aiding reproducibility of the math.
Numerical stability improvement over LCM is convincingly demonstrated with large-scale synthetic stress tests, addressing a genuine practical limitation of the popular LCM approach.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is somewhat incremental: once the block/product structure of the Cholesky metric is observed, applying known 1D metrics (power-Euclidean, Bures-Wasserstein) to the diagonal part is a relatively mechanical extension of existing pullback-metric machinery (Thanwerdas & Pennec, Han et al.).

Accuracy gains over strong baselines (LCM, AIM, LEM) are often modest or mixed (e.g., FPHA, Radar improvements are small, and θ-BWCM sometimes underperforms AIM/LEM), with the largest gains concentrated on HDM05 and reliant on per-dataset tuning of θ over an 11-point grid, raising concerns about fair comparison with untuned baselines.

The generalized (θ, M)-BWCM's extra parameter M shows only marginal impact per the ablation (Table 14), suggesting this generalization axis contributes little practical value and M=I is used throughout main experiments, weakening the significance of that contribution.

Experiments are limited to three relatively small/mid-scale benchmark datasets (Radar, HDM05, FPHA) typical of prior SPD network papers; no evaluation on larger-scale or more diverse tasks (e.g., large EEG, video, or vision benchmarks) to assess broader significance.
The swelling-effect comparison in tensor interpolation is only illustrated qualitatively on a single 3x3 example rather than systematically quantified across many matrix samples/dimensions.

Presentation is very dense with heavy notation and many theorem/lemma cross-references, which may hinder accessibility and reproducibility for readers not already deeply familiar with the Thanwerdas-Pennec/Lin/Han geometric frameworks.

GBWM, one of the six metrics discussed as directly relevant prior work, is not included as a baseline in the main classification experiments, leaving a gap in the comparison against the most closely related generalized metric.

strengths: Identifies a clean product-manifold decomposition of the Cholesky space (lower-triangular Euclidean part x n copies of R++), which is a nice unifying conceptual device for metric design.

Derives full closed-form Riemannian operators (geodesics, Log/Exp, parallel transport, Fréchet mean) and gyrovector-space structures for the two new metrics, with corresponding proofs in the appendix, which is technically thorough.

Extensive experimental suite: SPD MLR classifiers on two backbones (SPDNet, GyroSPD), residual networks, numerical-stability stress tests with extreme eigenvalue ranges, tensor-interpolation/swelling analysis, and scalability/runtime benchmarking up to 512-dim matrices.
Good reproducibility effort: detailed hyperparameters, dataset preprocessing, ablations on the deformation factor θ and the matrix M in BWCM, and complete proofs provided.
Addresses a genuine, previously documented weakness of LCM (numerical blow-up of diagonal log/exp for small eigenvalues) with a plausible, well-motivated fix (diagonal power vs. logarithm).
weaknesses: Core novelty is incremental: once the product structure of the Cholesky manifold is noted, plugging in known 1-D versions of existing SPD metrics (power-Euclidean, Bures–Wasserstein) to get PCM/BWCM is a fairly direct combination of prior techniques (Lin 2019, Thanwerdas & Pennec 2022, Han et al. 2023) rather than a fundamentally new geometric idea.

Empirical gains are inconsistent and sometimes marginal: BWCM underperforms AIM/LCM on several settings (e.g., Radar under SPDNet, FPHA under GyroSPD), and improvements over LCM on Radar/FPHA are small, undermining the claim of a clear, general advantage.

The deformation factor θ needs per-dataset, per-backbone tuning (Table 7) via grid search over an ad hoc range, with no principled selection rule; this contradicts the paper's 'simple and convenient' framing and adds a hidden hyperparameter-search cost not reflected in the efficiency comparisons.

The generalized M-BWCM variant, despite being emphasized theoretically, shows negligible or mixed practical benefit (Table 14), suggesting the extra generality (and associated theory) has limited real impact and the paper mostly relies on the M=I special case throughout.

Numerical stability experiments rely on synthetic matrices with artificially extreme eigenvalue ranges (down to 1e-30), which may not reflect realistic training dynamics; the connection between this synthetic stability advantage and actual improvements in network optimization/training curves is not directly shown.

Tensor interpolation results show that even the proposed PCM still exhibits 'some level of swelling' relative to LCM, partially undercutting the practical motivation for the new metric in this application.

Baselines in the main classification experiments are limited to AIM/LEM/LCM (and BWM/PEM only in scalability check); more recent competitive SPD metrics referenced in the introduction (e.g., GBWM, adaptive Log-Euclidean metrics) are not included as classification baselines, making the comparison less complete.
Datasets used (Radar, HDM05, FPHA) are small, standard legacy SPD benchmarks; the significance of the proposed metrics for larger-scale or more modern SPD learning tasks is not demonstrated.

Gyro-structure operations require manual numerical safeguards (clipping diagonal entries to avoid violating positivity constraints), indicating the practical robustness is less clean than advertised and depends on ad hoc fixes.

strengths: Identifies a clean and useful product-manifold structure underlying the Cholesky manifold (Euclidean strictly-lower-triangular part × n copies of R++), providing a principled and general design space for new SPD metrics rather than an ad hoc construction.

Proposes two new metrics (θ-PCM and (θ,M)-BWCM) with fully closed-form Riemannian operators (geodesics, log/exp maps, parallel transport, weighted Fréchet mean) and gyrovector operations, rigorously proven to satisfy gyrovector space axioms (Thms 3.7, 4.1).

Introduces a diagonal power deformation that smoothly interpolates between the new metrics and the well-established Log-Cholesky Metric, offering a principled and tunable trade-off with theoretical justification (Lem. 3.5).

Strong and broad empirical validation: SPD MLR classifiers and residual blocks on multiple backbones (SPDNet, GyroSPD, RResNet) across three datasets (Radar, HDM05, FPHA), consistently outperforming AIM/LEM/LCM baselines while matching or improving efficiency.

Thorough numerical stability analysis (synthetic geodesics with near-degenerate eigenvalues) convincingly demonstrates the practical benefit of replacing diagonal log/exp with diagonal power operations, with dramatic differences in failure rates.

Detailed complexity analysis (asymptotic + empirical wall-clock) substantiates efficiency claims, showing the new metrics scale better than eigen-based methods (AIM, BWM) and are competitive with or faster than LCM at scale.

Extensive ablations (θ sweep, M in BWCM, diagonal statistics analysis) and tensor interpolation experiments add depth and help explain when/why the deformation parameter matters, improving interpretability of the method.
Comprehensive and well-organized appendix with full proofs, reproducibility details, and dataset/implementation specifics supports rigor and reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution—replacing diagonal logarithm/exponentiation with diagonal power operations—is conceptually incremental relative to existing LCM and PEM/GBWM constructions, even though the product-structure framing and full operator suite are valuable.

The optimal deformation factor θ varies substantially and non-intuitively across datasets and backbones (Table 7, e.g., -1.5 to 0.75), indicating a nontrivial hyperparameter search is needed in practice, which partially undercuts the simplicity/practicality narrative.

Accuracy gains over LCM are sometimes modest or mixed (e.g., FPHA with θ-BWCM on SPDNet is roughly on par with LCM; Radar with θ-BWCM underperforms LCM/AIM in some settings), suggesting the practical benefit is dataset- and metric-choice dependent.
The learnable M in BWCM (Table 14, Sec. E.6) shows negligible or inconsistent benefit over M=I, raising questions about the practical value of the generalized (θ,M)-BWCM beyond the simpler θ-PCM.
Residual block comparison (Table 4) reports only a single best-of-three result rather than mean±std as used elsewhere, making this comparison less statistically rigorous than the rest of the paper.

The numerical stability experiments rely on synthetic worst-case scenarios (artificially tiny eigenvalues); while illustrative, it is unclear how often such extreme conditions arise in the real training regimes actually used in the classification experiments, leaving the practical impact of this stability advantage somewhat unquantified in the main learning tasks.
